412.t: First night at the Hickory House with Joe Marsala
412.s: Hodes calls Joe Marsala, who has Buddy Rich, Marty Marsala and Adele Girard. Hodes is shocked that people pay to listen, and Marsala hires him. He gets his first DownBeat write-up.
412.q: Nothing. I was in bad shape. We just had to scrape. So I went down and put my card in, but I knew Joe Mar[shall], I called him up. He says, come on down. So I went down to see what the street was. And this was my first shot.

412.t: First night at the Hickory House with Joe Marsala
412.s: Hodes calls Joe Marsala, who has Buddy Rich, Marty Marsala and Adele Girard. Hodes is shocked that people pay to listen, and Marsala hires him. He gets his first DownBeat write-up.
412.q: Nothing. I was in bad shape. We just had to scrape. So I went down and put my card in, but I knew Joe Marsala, I called him up. He says, come on down. So I went down to see what the street was. And this was my first shot.

924.t: Jug bands before and after McDonald
924.s: Allen and Jasper Taylor ask about earlier jug bands. Jones says only McDonald got fine jobs, including the Hippodrome in New York, before coming to Chicago.
924.q: That's the only one that I know of is Earl McDonnell. I know several that come up after he did, but I never did pay any attention to them, because they weren't the rich one, and they didn't get no jobs in the first beginning. They never was put out or hired for no fine jobs and things like that.…

1002.t: Grant Green, Hank Crawford and first gigs with Sun Ra
1002.s: On arriving in New York he worked with Grant Green, then Hank Crawford in 1963, and subbed with Sun Ra, who asked for imagery in solos.
1002.q: Oh when I first moved to New York I started working with Grant Green. Guitarist for Blue Note Records, he played bebop guitar. And he had Bob Cranshaw, Bob

937.t: First job with Tommy Turrentine, Booker Ervin and Rahsaan Roland Kirk
937.s: His early experience came in Tommy Turrentine's band, with J.C. Moses, Booker Ervin and later Rahsaan Roland Kirk passing through.
937.q: Early on, yeah, well at first, my first job was with Tommy Turrentine, who is Stanley Turrentine’s older brother. And J.C. Moses was in the band, and Booker Ervin was in the band, he’d just got out of the Air Force and was on his way to the Big Apple, New York. And after that Rahsann Roland Kirk…

749.t: Jazzmania, the pianists she worked with, and the Harlem organ group
749.s: House vocalist at Jazzmania, learning bandstand arranging from players like Bishop, Barron and Pullen; first record dates and a Harlem organ-group year.
749.q: ‘Twisted’ in D.” In D? And the piano player would go, “D?” You know you don’t mean F? You don’t mean B flat? You know what I mean? “You mean ‘Twisted’ in D?”

721.t: Moving to New York, Gil Evans and Blood, Sweat & Tears
721.s: Malone lists his instruments and bands, then tells how he crashed with Bob Burgess in New York and subbed for Hannibal Marvin Peterson with Gil Evans, meeting Howard Johnson and Sanborn. Talk of Fred Lipsius and Lou Marini at BS&T follows.
721.q: Well I played one instrument or another with somebody in my career. You know I was tenor sax soloist with Frank Zappa. I was a trumpet player with Blood, Sweat & Tears with Lew Soloff, 1973. And I played jazz tuba, I played on Howard Johnson’s last five tuba recordings. On and on and on.

344.s: A telegram from Golson brought him to New York, where the Birdland rehearsal turned out to be an audition he won.
344.ch: New York: Jazztet and sidemen years
344.q: No, what happened is we went to the Five Spot and played with the Brothers, and then I came back to Rochester and we went back into The Pythod. And I got a telegram from Benny Golson. And he said he wanted me to come to New York and join the Jazztet. And Tootie Heath was the drummer with the ‘tet…

784.t: Gretsch Drum Night and sitting in with Coltrane at Birdland
784.s: As a boy he worked weekends with Earl Swanson and Tiny Grimes, sat in at Birdland with Elvin Jones, Blakey, Roach and with Coltrane.
784.q: Swanson, not even, I was doing little weekend things because I was too young and at that time it was a cabaret license. And I went out on the road with Earl Swanson and the organ player was Don Pullen. He was playing Hammond organ. And then Tiny Grimes, that’s when I worked with Tiny Grimes at that…

586.t: Playing Sweet Basil's with Benny Waters
586.s: Her first public New York engagement was a week at Sweet Basil's with 95-year-old Benny Waters, after an intense rehearsal.
586.q: Well I really enjoyed performing last October down in New York with Benny Waters, the saxophone player, at Sweet Basil’s jazz club in New York. That was the first time I ever really publicly played in New York City and it was a week-long engagement. And I really enjoyed that. Really nice.

934.t: Arriving in New York in 1965 and joining the Elgart band
934.s: He sat in at jam sessions and The Dom, and got his first big band job with Les Elgart through another saxophonist.
934.q: It’s a good question. I’ll put it to you in a — people might be shocked in a sense, because you develop a history and people have a preconception. But when I came to New York in 1965 and I would go around and force myself to sit in jam sessions and places where it’s possible to sit in, just because…

989.t: Meeting Jackie McLean through Jim Harrison and the Blue Coronet
989.s: Jim Harrison sends Tolliver to Jackie McLean after a jam at the Blue Coronet in Brooklyn; McLean hears his tunes and books him for the next record date.
989.ch: First Blue Note recording with Jackie McLean
989.q: I’ll say this, at one point my knees were shaking you know. You know when I decided to leave Howard University with my pharmacy studies and grapple with this thing, that was the moment where I said I know I can do this. And so anything that came after that was like gravy for me because I, you know,…

552.t: Arriving in New York with Out of the Blue
552.s: He replaced Kenny Garrett in Out of the Blue, which had no work, and sat in with Faddis, Murray and Bluiett.
552.ch: Richmond and arriving in New York
552.q: Yeah. Fortunately. I had just joined a band called Out of the Blue, which was a young lions group put together by Blue Note Records at the time. And I replaced Kenny Garrett who had gone on to join Art Blakey and then subsequently Miles. So I was in that band when I got to New York but the band…

494.t: First New York gigs and James Moody's sextet
494.s: First gig at Birdland with Bill and Ted Curson, then work with Moody's sextet playing Tom McIntosh's music.
494.ch: Philadelphia roots and arrival in New York
494.q: A little bit, a little bit. My first gig in New York was, I think, a Monday night at Birdland with my brother and Ted Curson. That was my very first gig in New York. But I was starting to do little things, like coffee shops and things like that. I didn’t really start working – I think Dizzy…

515.s: Corea gets the piano chair in Blue Mitchell's group, having loved Blowin' The Blues Away.
515.q: Well, look at the fortuitousness of that, which is me in love with that band, Blowin’ The Blues Away. There’s that band, and when Horace wasn’t doing Horace Silver Quintet gigs, Blue would take the group and do gigs. He needed a piano player. I still can’t remember how I got that gig, but I ended…

504.t: Freelancing, Betty Carter, Don Pullen and forming the Charles Lloyd Quartet
504.s: He freelances with Betty Carter and others, remembers Don Pullen, and with Keith Jarrett and Cecil McBee helps form the Lloyd quartet.
504.ch: New York and the Lloyd quartet
504.q: Yeah, I'd like to check into that. So, I played with Jackie for a while and then I free-lanced a bit around New York. I played some with Sun Ra. I played with Betty Carter, John Hicks and Cecil McBee. I'd have to say about John Hicks and Don Pullen because both of those guys, I think John came from…

227.t: Back to New York with Chubby Jackson
227.s: In spring 1949 Mandel got a job in Chubby Jackson's swinging band at Bop City with Tiny Kahn.
227.ch: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
227.q: Yes, exactly, yeah around March or April, immediately got a job in Chubby Jackson's band up at Bop City with Tiny Kahn, you know a real swinging band. And that was, Woody was in-between bands at that time, he had broken up the Second Herd, the First Herd and hadn’t… wait a minute…

408.t: Early New York gigs: Monday nights at Birdland, Raney and Barnet
408.s: Jimmy Chapin's Monday Birdland band, the Goodstein family, first record with Jimmy Raney in 1954, and early work with Charlie Barnet and Neal Hefti.
408.ch: Breaking in: Birdland, Dizzy and Bird
408.q: Well I started to work at, I started to do Monday nights at Birdland, with Jimmy Chapin umm, Jim Chapin has, the son became a very successful pop singer [Harry Chapin] …

529.t: Back in New York, Kenny Dorham hears Sam at a session
529.s: After Bradshaw's death Sam plays sessions at the Paradise Club and Kenny Dorham invites him into the Jazz Prophets.
529.q: And that's how I really learned and from one thing led to another, like I said, from Bradshaw to the Jazz Prophets--that was my first big jazz gig.
